what_it_certifies: That sustained ingest against the embedded store holds its latency SHAPE over time, that the file grows in proportion to the data rather than faster, and that the journal sidecar stays bounded while the quiet-window maintenance pass runs alongside. These are properties of duration, not of any single change, which is why this lane runs on its own clock and never gates a merge.

workload.read_mix: cost_summary + list_events(200) in a loop, the dashboard shape
workload.maintenance: one quiet-window pass every 500ms, truncating once the journal passes 4 MiB
workload.shape_note: The real production mix is unknown — this instance has no fleet telemetry to shape the load from. One writer is not an approximation but a fact: the SQLite backend serialises writes behind one connection by design, so a second writer would measure queueing, not the store. An honest lane certifying a declared-approximate workload beats a confident lane certifying an unexamined one; when a real traffic profile exists, it replaces this block and the bounds are re-declared against it.

max_errors.predicate: store errors returned by insert_event_checked over the whole run. Committed work is never lost and never refused.

write_p95_ms.predicate: 95th percentile single-event write latency, at the declared concurrency, for the declared duration. A percentile and not an average: an average hides exactly the tail this lane exists to see.

write_p95_drift_ratio.predicate: p95 of the run's FINAL bucket divided by p95 of the first bucket of its second half - the slope measured WITHIN the second half, at the declared concurrency. The trend criterion: a p95 that sits under its ceiling at the finish is still compatible with linear degradation that clears the ceiling an hour later, so the slope is judged separately from the endpoint. Measured inside the second half rather than half-against-half because the opening bucket is cache warm-up, and folding warm-up into the numerator produces a ratio nobody can act on. Bounded at 3x rather than 1x because a growing file legitimately writes a little slower than an empty one.

db_bytes_per_event.predicate: database file bytes (page_count x page_size) divided by events written, measured at the end. Catches growth that is super-linear in the data — an index that fans out, a page-fragmentation spiral — as opposed to the file simply holding what was put in it.

wal_bytes_max.predicate: the largest journal sidecar observed at any sample during the run, in bytes (96 MiB). This is the criterion the quiet-window maintenance pass exists to hold: without a checkpoint the sidecar is what grows unattended, and retention being deliberately unbounded (operator 2026-08-24) makes it the one growth axis engineering still controls. Read it as a CEILING ON A PLATEAU, not as a race with the clock - see what_the_lane_measured_first.

bounds_are_declared_before_the_run: These numbers were fixed before the runs that judge them. Criteria adjusted while looking at results are not criteria; they are commentary. They are chosen loose enough to be stable on a shared CI runner and tight enough that the planted-defect run fails them — which is checked on every single run, not assumed.
how_the_bounds_were_calibrated: Arming a threshold without measuring what it will see is how a lane earns a reputation for crying wolf, so each bound was set against an observed baseline BEFORE any run judged it. First against the author's machine (2026-08-24, 30 s enforced: 10621 events, 0 errors, write p95 8.1 ms, drift 1.25x, 2494 bytes/event, peak journal 18.7 MiB). Then, the same day and still before the first nightly, against the environment that will actually judge them - two dispatched CI runs on a GitHub runner: 90 s (125361 events, p95 0.705 ms, drift 1.14x, 2480 bytes/event, peak journal 56.9 MiB) and 300 s (351019 events, 0 errors, p95 0.74 ms, drift 1.24x, 2481 bytes/event, peak journal 58.4 MiB). Both passed. That second measurement moved exactly one bound: wal_bytes_max from 64 MiB to 96 MiB, because 64 left 9% headroom over a real observation and a lane that goes red on its first nightly for a runner-to-runner difference is a lane nobody will trust by its third. Nothing else moved - latency and per-event growth came in an order of magnitude INSIDE their bounds on CI, and loosening a bound the evidence does not push on would be commentary. Re-declaring a bound against the judging environment before it judges is calibration; changing one after reading a verdict you did not like is not, and this paragraph exists so the difference stays visible. When a bound changes, this paragraph changes with it and says what was measured.
what_the_lane_measured_first: The lane's first CI runs, 2026-08-24, produced a finding before they produced a verdict: under CONTINUOUS read load the journal does not grow without bound, and it does not stay small either - it plateaus. Two runs on the same GitHub runner, 90 s (125361 events, peak journal 56.9 MiB) and 300 s (351019 events, peak journal 58.4 MiB), agree within 3% despite the second doing 2.8x the work. That duration-independence is the finding: a passive or truncating checkpoint cannot advance past a live reader's snapshot, so with two reader threads looping without a gap the checkpointer starves and the sidecar settles at whatever the starvation dynamics allow rather than at whatever the write rate would imply. The bound is therefore a ceiling on that plateau (96 MiB, ~1.6x the observed steady state) and not a budget that a longer run must be granted more of - and a regression that actually broke checkpointing would leave the plateau behind entirely and blow through it in seconds. In production this is the case the maintenance ladder's escalated rung exists for: continuous traffic means the activity gauge never reads zero, so the sweep defers, and it is the journal's own byte bound that then fires and runs the pass regardless (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md section 12).

lane_health.green_on_known_good: asserted every run: the good-configuration run must satisfy every criterion above
lane_health.red_on_known_bad: asserted every run: a second run with a deliberate latency injection in its second half must FAIL, and must fail on write_p95_drift_ratio specifically. A lane that has never been observed to fail for cause is indistinguishable from a lane that cannot fail; one that fails for the wrong reason certifies nothing.
lane_health.first_green: 2026-08-24 (local, enforced, 30 s/phase); first green in CI the same day, dispatched, at 90 s and 300 s per phase - runs 32778684961 and 32780650640)
